summary.value: Thus, while rapamycin does not acutely inhibit mTORC2, when high doses of rapamycin treatment are continued for a prolonged period of time, mTORC2 activity is decreased, most likely due to rapamycin sequestering free mTOR and hindering the formation of new mTORC2 [56].

scope.value: Treatments that expose subjects to rapamycin intermittently, especially at low doses, compared with daily treatment. The author states that the reduced side effects with continued lifespan extension have been shown in mice. Because intermittent treatment also inhibits mTORC1 less, it could be less efficacious in promoting healthy aging.

text.value: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 by binding FKBP12, and the complex binds the FRB domain of mTOR; the FRB domain is exposed in mTORC1 but buried in mTORC2 by mTORC2-specific proteins such as Rictor.
text.basis_quote: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 by first binding to FK506-binding protein 12 (FKBP12); this complex in turn then binds to the FKBP12-rapamycin-binding (FRB) domain of mTOR [51, 52]. While the FRB is located on the surface of mTORC1, in mTORC2 it is buried by proteins such as Rictor which are specific to mTORC2 [53–55].

value.note: The article (paragraph 24) says the author hypothesized the claim and shows it with refs. 34 and 68. Ref. 68 (Aging Cell) states the hypothesis that different dosing schedules might expand the therapeutic window by more specifically targeting mTORC1 (paragraph 3); the date is its electronic publication date. Ref. 34 (J Gerontol A 2016, the lifespan study) was not read. What the search layer of 2026-10-21 found no earlier statement of, in five query families on two services in both orders, is the mTORC2-sparing rationale - that an intermittent schedule works by inhibiting mTORC1 while largely sparing mTORC2. It is not a measured absence of the lifespan claim itself: the same calls (509085e70ad3, 84ec3c1cc3e9) return at rank 3 PMID 24556924 / PMC4026081 (2014), "Lifespan extension and cancer prevention in HER-2/neu transgenic mice treated with low intermittent doses of rapamycin", a year earlier. Its licence is unestablished rather than refused: the null in the log comes from PubMed esummary records, which carry no licence field at all, and that work has no Europe PMC record and no status call of its own, so this card neither reads nor quotes it. Two further earlier statements are in a work this card does read: Blagosklonny 2019 (PMC6690951) says intermittent administration was proposed in 2008 (its ref. 138) and that weekly rapamycin for 22 weeks inhibited mTORC1 while "mTORC2 activity remained intact" in 2014 (its ref. 70). So the date here is the one the converted article attributes to the hypothesis as it states it, and not a claim that no part of it was stated earlier.

summary.value: Rapamycin binds FKBP12, and the complex binds the FRB domain of mTOR. The FRB domain is on the surface of mTORC1 but buried in mTORC2 by mTORC2-specific proteins such as Rictor, so rapamycin does not acutely inhibit mTORC2. When high doses are continued for a prolonged time, mTORC2 activity falls, most likely because rapamycin sequesters free mTOR and hinders the formation of new mTORC2; acute treatment inhibits mTORC1, chronic treatment both complexes.

Nothing in this card is retracted. The status of its five sources is a different question, and it was checked: twelve status calls, one per source and one for a notice the calls found (search-log.jsonl). Eleven returned no notice. One did: Minton et al. 2021 (PMC8495984), the work behind e_oa_mtorc2_intact, carries a correction notice (MED:35016718, 10.1186/s13075-022-02718-9, 2022-01-11), which was fetched and read - it corrects the spelling of an author's name and changes no result this card quotes - and is recorded in that line's risk-of-bias note. An earlier version of this reason said no source carried a notice of any kind, written while that call's record had been read down to its `outcome` and `found` fields, neither of which carries a notice: the notice is in its `status` and `notices`. The conditions of the claim are in core.scope and in the eight assumptions, each with the paragraph that states it. The article declares no separate typed context, and splitting its prose into typed qualifiers would be the converter's reading, not the author's.
The eight assumptions are the author's own statements, quoted in their basis quotations. The converter made no assessment of its own about them.

a_general is the hypothesis as the author states it and the other atoms are its parts, but the article does not build that hierarchy: it states the parts and the whole in one sentence. A parent the converter chose would be a structure the source does not have.
No atom is a typed compound of other atoms, so none carries an operator.
Every atom holds in the scope the card states; none is restricted to a narrower context.

The article states no result that would count against the claim. It states the opposite risk — that intermittent dosing could be less efficacious because it inhibits mTORC1 less — and that is carried as the prediction p_intermittent_vs_daily and the uncertainty u_efficacy_dose, not as a falsification condition the author did not set.

The benefit the article names is of the research programme, not of this hypothesis being true: that rapamycin or molecules acting similarly on mTOR may yet extend healthspan and lifespan (paragraph 2). A potential benefit record needs the outcome, who it is for and its constraints, and the article states them for rapamycin in general rather than for the intermittent schedule.

The author claims the hypothesis and its mouse demonstration as his own (paragraph 24, refs. 34 and 68) but states no bounded new-versus-shared content, and this field needs retained search or review evidence for that split. The search layer of 2026-10-21 measured where the article stands (0 citing works, 0 responses, 0 notices — a 2026 review) and that does not establish what is new.
The card is about an effect of a schedule, not a rate in a reference class; the article gives no denominator for any rate it reports.

The one finding the article reinterprets is off this card's axis: it suggests the paradoxical rise in plasma Abeta40 and Abeta42 under rapamycin could reflect material flowing out of brain plaques (paragraph 47). That is a reinterpretation about Alzheimer biomarkers, not about the mTORC2-sparing claim, and the converter will not attach it to an atom it does not bear on.

The mechanism summary is the author's own and names each step of it; no step is left as a box whose interior the article declines to state. What is missing is the typed form of the steps, which completeness.missing_for_next records.

No source attaches an uncertainty to a prediction. The one the author does state — that intermittent dosing could be less efficacious — is itself a prediction here (p_intermittent_vs_daily) and an uncertainty of the card (u_efficacy_dose).

The INDRA epistemics flag marks a statement extracted as a hypothesis rather than a result. Every line here is a reported result of its own source; the author's confidence is carried where a reader expects it, in each atom's modality with the hedge quoted.

No line reports a negated statement. The measured nulls — no effect of intermittent rapamycin on glucose tolerance, no difference in glucose metabolism in Queiroz et al. — are findings in their own right, with their direction toward the target atom stated.
No passage of the five sources states an interval for the result the line reports.

What each analysis was is already in the line's study_type, which the entailment pass checks against the same passage. A second typed field saying it again would be checked against the same sentence twice without adding anything a reader could not read there.

Evidence strength is an assessment, and the converter makes only the two it can ground: indirectness, from the distance between the study and the claim, and risk of bias, where a source states the ground for it (the self-selected survey population, the compounded doses of PEARL, the non-significant between-group comparisons of the daily trial). It will not score strength on a scale the standard deliberately does not define.

Checked and recorded elsewhere, not withheld: eight status calls, one per source - five on 2026-10-21 and three on 2026-10-22, after three further works entered the card - found no retraction, correction or expression of concern for any source (all none_found, search-log.jsonl), and the article's own Crossref check is in added.source_verification.metadata_check. One line comes close and is not a replication: Queiroz et al. used the every-five-days regimen of Arriola Apelo et al. in a different strain (SAMP8) for a different purpose, which the card records as a separate independence group with its own indirectness, not as a replication record.

There is no evidence.references entry. The licence under which each of the five sources was read is in INPUTS-20261021.md and, for the works that entered later, in the report, each from that file's own permissions block.

There is an interest to declare and OHF 1.0 has nowhere to put it. The article's own competing-interest statement (paragraph 100) reads: "DWL has received funding from, and is a scientific advisory board member of, Aeovian Pharmaceuticals, which seeks to develop novel, selective mTOR inhibitors for the treatment of various diseases." That bears directly on a card whose hypothesis argues for selective mTORC1 inhibition. This field is for a cited work in evidence.references, not for the main source, and the provenance layer has no field for it; the declaration is therefore in this reason, in the report, and nowhere else the standard provides.

A citation search of three services (Europe PMC, PubMed and OpenAlex) over four seed works, read 1,395 citing works by title, 68 by abstract, and named sixteen works against this card that were in neither the card nor its leads; seven of those bear directly on an atom. Three of the seven could be read under the licence rule and two are now lines of this card (e_oa_mtorc2_intact from PMC8495984 and e_blago_transplant from PMC6690951, both CC BY). The third, PMC9652467 (Xie et al. 2022, deep phenotyping: lifespan interventions act in age-independent ways rather than slowing the rate of age-dependent change), is CC BY and read, and is carried here rather than as a line because what it disputes is the healthspan premise, which this card holds as the assumption as_healthspan_in_mice, and a line can target an atom, a mechanism step or a prediction, not an assumption. Four of the seven could not be read: PMID 31276577 / PMC6909913 and PMID 23648089 / PMC3727050 (glucose intolerance with insulin sensitivity preserved, attributed to insulin secretion) have no licence in the record; PMID 34389472 (impaired bone accrual under every-other-day dosing, the one direct objection to the intermittent schedule itself) is CC BY but has no PMC record, so the route this card uses reaches no text; PMID 40394335 / PMC12092812 (a phase 1 of 1 mg daily in people: HbA1c and systolic pressure up, cerebrospinal p-tau181, GFAP and NfL up) is CC BY-NC-ND and may not be quoted. The nine works that limit the scope rather than contradict a claim are named in the report with the same kind of reason. The counts of the conversion's own searches exist and are not in the card: every call of this conversion is in search-log.jsonl with the sha256 of every response, five query families run twice on two services, four of them returning nothing with their call ids, 100 similar candidates narrowed to 25. The counts themselves are in the report, with the sha256 of the log as it stood at handover, because the log keeps growing while the conversion runs - the entity lookups write to it too - and a count written into the card would be stale by the next run. Works that wave 3 named as fetchable and that are not in the card are listed in the report as known and not read, with their identifiers; so is Blagosklonny 2012 (PMC3384435), which is CC BY 2.5 - a licence the released kit does not accept, though it permits republication with attribution - and which is therefore a lead this conversion could not use. The field is a sourced value, and the kit can bind a value only to a paragraph of a source document, not to its own search log.

entailment.note: The passage supports only the T-cell/mTORC2 alternative; it says nothing about the calorie-restriction-mimetic label or about broader mTORC1 inhibitors such as NR1, Rapalink-1 and RMC-5552.

The passage says nothing about human studies being small or short-term or about a critical need for larger and longer studies (u_small_short_studies), and it does not say that an intermittent low-dose regimen cannot be distinguished from a lower one when bioavailability is unknown (the u_drug_sourcing consequence).
The passage supports the hepatic-insulin-resistance/glucose-intolerance observation but says nothing about intermittent dosing or a reduced-but-significant residual effect on T cells.
The passage says only that rapamycin's immunosuppression depends in part on mTORC2 suppression; it says nothing about intermittent treatment being less immunosuppressive.
The passage never mentions intermittent dosing or compares schedules; it attributes deregulated nutrient sensing only to long-term high-dose rapamycin.
The passage does not say what dosing regimen the cold-challenged mice received, so it cannot dispute a claim specific to intermittent low-dose treatment.

The passage's claim is hedged ('likely have decreased resilience to fasting') and inferred from leanness, and it states no dosing schedule, so it does not contradict a claim specific to intermittent low-dose treatment.
The passage reports impaired wound and fracture healing for rapamycin in general without stating any dose or schedule, so it does not speak to intermittent low-dose treatment.

The passage reports impaired infection response and adaptive immunity for rapamycin without stating a dosing schedule or any mTORC2 measurement, so it does not contradict the hedged claim about intermittent treatment.

The passage gives no dose or schedule for the human rapamycin and rapalog use behind the increased infection risk, so it does not contradict a claim limited to intermittent low doses under medical supervision.
The passage never names the species or model studied, so the recorded system: some grade has no visible grounds in it.
The passage says only that the rapamycin was low-dose over 48 weeks; it does not state that dosing was intermittent or that use was under medical supervision.

The passage reports deleterious osteoarthritis effects of rapamycin but says nothing about intermittent dosing or low doses, so it does not bear on the schedule-and-dose qualification of the statement.

The passage reports some statistically significant marker changes in single dose/sex subgroups but states that most values did not change and that all observed changes stayed within normal result windows, so it does not support a finding that counts against few adverse events under supervised low-dose use without that qualification.
The passage describes a 48-week trial cohort with 5 mg and 10 mg groups and sex-stratified blood-panel analyses but never states that participants were randomized or that dosing was weekly.
The passage supports males in the 5 mg cohort but gives no dosing schedule, so the "weekly" qualifier is unsupported.
The passage is consistent with a trial report paragraph but contains nothing identifying the file PMC12074816.xml, its sha256 digest, or its position as the 22nd paragraph.

The passage reports within-cohort change in blood biomarkers over time with no dosing schedule and no placebo contrast, so grades of "none" for endpoint, intervention, and comparison indirectness relative to a claim about adverse events under intermittent low-dose use are unsupported.
The passage names no study, trial, author, or cohort identity, so it gives no basis for the independence group label "g_pearl".

The passage shows intermittent (every-other-month) eRapa extending lifespan but compares schedules, not doses, so it does not support the statement's 'especially at low doses' qualifier (nor state the species of the present study's animals).

For the present study the passage says only 'both males and females' and 'either sex'; it names mice only in the three previously published studies it cites, so the species of this study's animals is not stated.
The passage is plain prose that carries no filename, no sha256 digest and no paragraph index, so it cannot confirm the artifact 'PMC7681050.xml', its hash, or the locator 'XML .//p[21]'.

The 'intervention: some' grade has visible grounds in the eRapa-diet schedules, but 'system: none' rests on a species the passage never states for this study and 'comparison: none' on a control group the passage never mentions.
The passage shows one study comparing three arms in parallel but says nothing about the Interventions Testing Program or a 2020 report, so it gives no grounds for the group label 'g_itp_dosing_2020'.

The note's figures (15%, 8%, 4% and each protocol differing from the other two in females) are stated, but the passage reports only effect sizes and p-values and says nothing about randomisation, blinding, attrition or other study conduct that would ground a risk-of-bias level of 'some'.
The passage disputes low-dose efficacy only for males at 4.7 ppm in the pooled data, while females benefited at even the lowest dose, and it examines no intermittent schedule.

The passage establishes a mouse study with a direct intermittent-versus-continuous comparison, but it names no target claim against which the endpoint and intervention could be graded as partially indirect ('some') while the system is graded 'none'.

The passage establishes a mouse study with a direct intermittent-versus-continuous comparison, but it names no target claim against which the endpoint and intervention could be graded as partially indirect ('some') while the system is graded 'none'.

The passage supports a controlled comparison (hence comparison "none") and an animal system, but it names no target claim against which the "some" grades for endpoint and intervention indirectness could be judged.
The passage reports no measurement of the mediating mechanism and no controlled comparison of its own, so it gives no clear grounds for rating the endpoint and comparison merely "some" indirect.

The quoted sentence is verbatim from the passage, but the one-sentence passage gives no grounds for a "high" bias level and says nothing about whether rapamycin's glucose intolerance is a harm, which the note asserts is what it bears on.
The passage carries no information about a file name, checksum or paragraph position, so it cannot support the artifact, sha256 or locator.

The passage gives grounds for some endpoint and intervention indirectness (pan-mTOR inhibitor standing in for rapamycin), but not for rating the study system as "none" when much of the cited evidence is in mice, and it says nothing about comparators that would support "serious" comparison indirectness.
The passage names no author, group or year, so it gives no grounds for this independence-group identifier.

The passage gives no grounds for a neutral direction overall: alongside the absence of cognitive change it reports significant increases in CSF tau-181, GFAP and neurofilament light, plus higher systolic blood pressure and HbA1c and lower erythrocyte parameters.

The passage disputes rapamycin-induced systemic insulin resistance but never mentions mTORC2, the liver or hepatic insulin resistance, so it gives no grounds for a verdict on that specific mechanistic atom.

The passage reports harm under an every-other-day 4 mg/kg regimen but never compares intermittent with continuous dosing or low with high doses, so it gives no grounds for disputing a claim specifically about intermittent, low-dose treatment having reduced side effects, and it hedges its own conclusion with "may".

The passage describes continuous daily dosing (1 mg/day for eight weeks), not intermittent dosing, and reports twenty adverse events together with significant biomarker, blood-pressure and HbA1c increases, so it does not support the 'few adverse events' framing as a neutral result.
The passage reports an impact on T cells and the immune system but gives no molecular measurement, so it does not support classifying this endpoint as "molecular".
